Stage 3 · Grammar

used to

Something that was true once, and is not true now.

Read these four sentences from the text.
  • People used to read a weekly paper, not a daily one.
  • Newspapers that used to appear once a week began to appear every morning.
  • They used to know less, but they used to feel calmer.
  • Did you use to read a printed newspaper?
In all four sentences, what does used to tell you about now?
The three forms
 FormExample
Positiveused to + plain verbI used to buy a paper every Sunday.
Negativedidn’t use to + plain verbI didn’t use to read the news at all.
QuestionDid … use to + plain verbDid you use to watch the news?
Short answersYes, I did. / No, I didn’t.
Every personI / you / he / she / we / they used to… — the form never changes.
The d disappearsused to → after did it is use to: didn’t use to, Did you use to…? ✗ didn’t used to
Only the pastThere is no present form. For now, say I usually read it online.
used to or the past simple?
 Use it when…Example
used toit was a habit or a state, repeated or lasting, and it has changedI used to live in Almaty. (I don’t now)
Past Simpleit happened once, or you say exactly how long or how many timesI lived in Almaty for three years. · I moved there in 2016.
Both possibleI used to walk to school. / I walked to school every day. — both correct; used to adds “not any more”.
used to / use to the plain verb

FORM. used to + the plain verb. Same for every person.

USE. A past habit or a past state that is no longer true. That second half is the whole point.

THE D. After did the d goes: didn’t use to, Did you use to…?

Not “I used to went”, not “I didn’t used to”, not “Did you used to”, not “I use to live here” about now.

There is no slider recording for this form in Unit 11. Read the four examples aloud yourself, twice.

FORM. used to + the plain form of the verb: I used to read, she used to live, they used to be. It is the same for every person — there is no he uses to, ever.

USE. It marks something that was a habit or a situation in the past and is not true now. I used to smoke tells the listener two things at once: I smoked then, and I do not smoke today. If it is still true, you cannot use this form — say I still smoke or I usually…

THE MISSING D. In the negative and the question, did already carries the past, so the d drops: I didn’t use to like coffee. Did you use to walk to school? In speech used to and use to sound identical, which is exactly why the spelling catches people out in writing.

AGAINST THE PAST SIMPLE. Both are correct English and the difference is meaning, not grammar. I used to live in Almaty = a period that is over, no dates given. I lived in Almaty for three years = you are counting the time, so the past simple. If you name a single occasion — I moved there in 2016 — used to is impossible: it was not a habit.

Four mistakes to watch: “I used to went” (the verb stays plain) · “I didn’t used to” (drop the d) · “Did you used to?” (drop it here too) · “I use to live here” meaning now (there is no present form).

One thing to file away. With states — be, have, know, like — only used to works: I used to have long hair. You may meet would used the same way for repeated actions (we would walk home together), but never for states.

Read each one aloud before you move on.

Full grammar reference — used to

Form

PositiveI used to play football every day.
NegativeI didn’t use to like coffee.
QuestionDid you use to walk to school?
Short answersYes, I did. / No, I didn’t.
The alternativewould also describes repeated past actions, but not past states.

Spelling and sound

No -d after did: didn’t use to, Did you use to…? The -d only appears in the positive.

When and why we use it

  • Used to describes a habit or a state that was true in the past and is not true now.
  • It works with states as well as actions: I used to have long hair.
  • For something that is still true, use the Present Simple: I still walk to work.
  • The Past Simple is also correct; used to adds the idea that the situation has changed.

Signal words

in those days · when I was young · years ago · not any more · no longer

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I didn’t used to like coffee. → I didn’t use to like coffee.No -d after did.
  • I use to play football. → I used to play football.The positive keeps the -d.
  • I am used to walk to school. → I used to walk to school.Be used to is a different structure.
  • Did you used to smoke? → Did you use to smoke?Same rule in questions.

Don’t confuse it with

I used to swim = a past habit that stopped. I’m used to swimming = it is normal for me now. Different structures; do not mix them.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

How long the news used to take, and what changed.

Before you read: two hundred years ago, how long did news take to travel from one town to the next?

Decide first. The answer is in the first paragraph.

How the news used to travel

Two hundred years ago, news moved at the speed of a horse. A robbery in one town used to take three days to reach the next. People used to read a weekly paper, not a daily one, and by the time an article about a flood or a forest fire arrived, the water had gone down and the fire was out. Nobody expected anything else.

Then came the telegraph. From the 1840s, messages ran along wires almost as fast as light. A hurricane in one country could be reported in another the same afternoon. Newspapers that used to appear once a week began to appear every morning, and the men who set up those first daily papers became rich. Editors who used to wait weeks for the post now waited minutes for the wire.

Today a crash, a strike or an election result reaches a phone in seconds. That is not only good news. When a volcano erupts we find out at once — but we also find out about a thousand things that will never matter to us. People who grew up before the internet often say the same thing: they used to know less, but they used to feel calmer. If you could choose, would you go back?

One detail is easy to miss. The telegraph did not only make the news faster; it made it shorter. Sending a message cost money by the word, so reporters learned to cut everything that was not necessary. The short, flat sentence of modern news writing was invented by people trying to save a few coins.

Sources. Written for this course from published media history: T. Standage, The Victorian Internet · Reuters Institute, Digital News Report. Dates are approximate.

Asking — Did you use to…? · What did you use to…? · Was there a … when you were young? · And do you still…?
